title: Bust of Nefertiti
museum: Ägyptisches Museum und Papyrussammlung, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin (Neues Museum)
date: c. 1351–1334 BC (reign of Amenhotep IV/Akhenaten), 18th Dynasty
material: Limestone, painted; gypsum plaster, rock crystal, wax
license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (license assigned by the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin; NonCommercial + ShareAlike)

facts: Found in 1912 at Amarna by Ludwig Borchardt's German excavation, in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose.
Made of painted limestone with a gypsum plaster layer; the one inlaid eye is rock crystal.
Her left eye has no inlay.
notes: The official museum scan (6.4M triangles, full color), decimated to 200k with its color texture kept (2048px JPEG). The museum's CC license text is carved into the underside of the mesh. Non-commercial use only; derivatives must stay CC BY-NC-SA. Some commentators (and Creative Commons) dispute whether a museum can claim copyright over a scan of a public-domain object, but I used the license as stated. Native scan units are mm, so real scale is preserved.

facts: Found at Saqqara (mastaba C 8) and dates to about 2470 BC in the 5th Dynasty.
Workers at the excavation nicknamed him 'Sheikh el-Beled' (village headman) because he looked like their own village chief.
The original is carved from wood. The staff he once held is missing.

attribution: 3D scan of a plaster cast: Statens Museum for Kunst (SMK), Copenhagen, Royal Cast Collection (Den Kongelige Afstøbningssamling). Attribution not required; credit appreciated.
facts: Servant statues like this were placed in Old Kingdom tombs to provide food for the dead person in the afterlife.
She is grinding grain on a stone quern. Flour and grain were the basis of bread and beer, the two staples of the Egyptian diet.
notes: This is a scan of SMK's plaster CAST of the original, not the ancient object itself. Scan units unknown; scaled so height equals the cast's catalogued height. Untextured (geometry only). title: Kylix (two-handled drinking cup)
museum: Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum
date: Greek; date uncertain (the museum metadata says ca. 800 BC, which is early for a kylix)
license: CC0 1.0 (Smithsonian Open Access)
attribution: Kylix, Greece, Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, 1971-48-12, gift of Ruth Vollmer. 3D model: Smithsonian 3D Digitization, CC0.
facts: A kylix is a shallow, two-handled cup that Greeks used for drinking wine at symposia (drinking parties).
notes: Scanned and textured by the Smithsonian (CC0). The date and donor come from Smithsonian metadata as mirrored on Zenodo (record 21489107), because the Smithsonian Open Access API was rate-limited (DEMO_KEY) when I tried to confirm them directly. A date of 800 BC is early for the kylix shape, so check it before quoting. Scan units were mm, so real scale is preserved (0.22 m across the handles, 0.074 m tall). There was no genuine Egyptian beer or wine jar I could download without a login; this is the best real, openly licensed drinking vessel I found.
